title: Name every build, and upgrade a running identity install in place with a way back
blocked_by: DIRECTORY-044 landed on main (it adds the exit and readiness waits this brief's upgrade uses): the build starts only when `git log --oneline origin/main --grep=DIRECTORY-044` names its R1 and R2 commits.
purpose: A person running the identity product cannot tell which build is running, and cannot take a newer one: install only fills in what is missing and never restarts. So every landing stays invisible until someone swaps binaries by hand. This brief makes every binary name its commit and gives the product one command that upgrades a running install and puts the previous build back if the new one fails. Amended 28 September 2026 20:35 by Waffles after Archie's review of the first round (card/DIRECTORY-045 ca11e605): an upgrade that leaves the configuration and compose files behind cannot move an install to any build that adds a configuration key (the server refuses unknown keys), and so cannot carry the sign-in cookie fix, which lives in the compose file; an install made before this card must move to it; and an upgrade stopped part-way must be recoverable.
task: Stamp the build commit into every Lys binary, add `lys identity upgrade`, surface the running build in /authority and the screens, and prove the upgrade on a scratch install in the round, with the live install upgraded and recorded by the landing lead after landing.

requirements.title: `lys identity upgrade` swaps the binaries and screens and returns to the previous build on failure
requirements.spec: Behavioural. A new verb `lys identity upgrade --from DIR [--surface PKG] [--root ROOT]`. It refuses by name when ROOT holds no install, when DIR lacks any installed binary, or when a binary's --version cannot be read. It prints the installed and the new commit of each. It stops the service and then the broker, each waiting on its exit event through DIRECTORY-044's exit wait (never a sleep or a timeout); moves bin/ to bin.previous/ (replacing an older bin.previous/) and places the new binaries by copy to a temporary name and rename; places the screens package through the install's existing verify-and-place path when --surface is given, keeping the previous one the same way; starts the broker and then the service and waits for each ready on its readiness event. If a start or readiness fails, it stops what it started, restores bin.previous/ (and the previous screens), starts them, waits for them ready, and exits non-zero naming the failing binary and its log. It never touches data/ or credentials; the configuration and compose files move with the binaries as R5 says.
acceptance: A test on a scratch root installs build A (two stub binaries answering --version and readiness), upgrades to build B, and shows B running and A kept in bin.previous/; a second test where B's service exits before ready shows A restored, running and ready, and the named failure.
A test shows data/ and every credential are byte-identical before and after both upgrades.
grep -nE 'sleep|timeout' over the new files prints nothing.

files_changed.note: The upgrade verb. It refuses by name, prints installed and new commits, stops on exit events, swaps bin/ and the screens, starts, and waits on readiness events. On failure it puts the previous build back, naming the binary and its log.
Tests that A goes to B with A kept, that a B that exits early restores A, that data and credentials are untouched, and that refusals stop nothing.
`lys identity upgrade --from DIR [--surface PKG] [--root ROOT]`.

dev.how: It refuses before stopping anything when ROOT holds no install, when DIR lacks a binary, or when a new binary's --version is unreadable. It stops the service and then the broker through DIRECTORY-044's exit wait. bin/ moves to bin.previous/, and each new binary is copied under a temporary name and renamed into place. The screens go through the existing verify-and-place path. Readiness waits on log lines and the answer event, never on time. On failure it stops what it started, restores bin.previous/ and the previous screens, starts them, waits for ready, and exits non-zero naming the binary and log. Evidence: upgrade_tests.rs:18 an_upgrade_runs_the_new_build_and_keeps_the_previous, :101 a_service_that_exits_before_ready_puts_the_previous_build_back, :171 neither_upgrade_touches_data_or_a_credential and :194 refusals_are_named_and_stop_nothing. requirements.title: Prove the upgrade on a scratch install in the round, and on the live install after landing
requirements.spec: Evidence, in two parts. In the round: the upgrade tests drive `upgrade` end to end against a scratch install each test makes in its own temporary directory (build A's binaries running with the configuration and compose files A renders, then build B's), through the engine that brings the compose services to their definition, so neither a container runtime nor the live install is needed. The build machine has neither, and the round never reaches the live install or its state directory. After landing: the lead who lands the card upgrades the live install with the landed build's `lys identity upgrade --from`, and commits docs/design/directory/PROOF-UPGRADE.md to main naming the installed commit before, the landed commit after, the upgrade's printed lines, the `build` member of http://localhost:8490/api/authority, and the cookie setting in the install's compose environment. Secrets and passwords never appear in it. The live install was made before this card (R6), so that upgrade starts with its first move. The round does not write PROOF-UPGRADE.md.

requirements.title: The first move of an install made before this card
requirements.spec: Behavioural. An install with no install/build.json (made before this card) is upgraded, not re-installed: upgrade reads the placed binaries' versions (a binary that cannot answer --version is recorded as 'built before build stamps'), stops the processes its pid files name through their exit locks, or through the pid when a process has no exit lock, naming which, and proceeds as R2 and R5. Install run again never leaves a process running from a binary it replaced: it stops and restarts any process whose binary it changed, so install/build.json always names what runs. The binaries placed before this card have no build stamp. lys-identity-server reads --version as a configuration path and fails, and lys, lys-secrets and lys-home refuse it as an unexpected argument. Any installed binary whose --version exits non-zero or prints no stamp is recorded as 'built before build stamps' and the upgrade carries on. It is refused version_unreadable only for a binary in the new build folder.
acceptance: A scratch install laid out as before this card (no build.json, no exit locks, a binary without --version) is upgraded, and /api/authority answers the new commit.
Install run again with a changed binary restarts that process, and build.json equals the running build.

A test places an installed lys-identity-server stub that fails when given --version as a configuration path and a lys stub that exits 2 with an unexpected argument, and the upgrade records both as 'built before build stamps' and carries on to the new build.

files_changed.note: Adopts an install made before build stamps. commit_or_unstamped records an installed binary whose --version exits non-zero or prints no stamp as UNSTAMPED, 'built before build stamps', while a binary in the new build folder is still refused version_unreadable. A binary missing from bin/ is adopted from its running process. A process without an exit lock is stopped through its pid, with its exit waited on as an event and the route named.

binaries_that_fail_at_version_are_recorded_unstamped_and_upgraded, added in review and kept, covers acceptance row 3. unstamped_build writes a lys-secrets stub that exits 2 on an unexpected --argument and a lys-identity-server stub that takes --version as its configuration path and exits 1. The test asserts both are VersionUnreadable with exit statuses 2 and 1, that the upgrade prints 'installed built before build stamps, new B' for each, that both run B, and that build.json names B.
Install run again stops and restarts a process whose binary it changed, so build.json names what runs.
The upgrade reads the installed build through adopt::installed and stops units through adopt::stop.

dev.how: For an install with no build.json, adopt::installed reads each placed binary through commit_or_unstamped. A version_unreadable result, whether a non-zero exit or no stamp, is recorded as 'built before build stamps', and the upgrade continues through R2 and R5. Only a binary in the new build folder is refused version_unreadable. adopt::stop stops a process through its exit lock when it has one. Otherwise it stops it through its pid, waiting on a pidfd or the platform exit waiter, and says which route it took. Install run again restarts any process whose binary it replaced. Evidence: adopt_tests.rs:99 an_install_made_before_this_card_is_upgraded_and_answers_the_new_build (no build.json, no exit locks, a binary without --version; /api/authority answers B), :154 install_run_again_restarts_a_process_whose_binary_it_placed (build.json equals the running build) and :281 binaries_that_fail_at_version_are_recorded_unstamped_and_upgraded (row 3). The stubs sit in bin/, so no adoption path is taken. adopt_tests.rs is 317 lines. I did not run it: the brief forbids test commands in this seat, so the round's tests and clippy legs will be its first run.

requirements.title: An upgrade stopped part-way is finished or put back
requirements.spec: Behavioural. Before the first stop, an upgrade writes an intent record (install/upgrade.json: from and to builds, and each step as it completes, written by a temporary name and a rename). Every later upgrade, --back or install first reads it and, when present, finishes the recorded upgrade or puts the previous build back, naming which, before doing anything else. Each placed binary and file is read back and its digest compared with its source before the old one is removed, as the screens already are. A readiness check on a process already running reads its log from the offset it opened at, never from the first byte on each change. upgrade.rs stays under 500 lines by moving the swap, render and adopt into their own modules.
